solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Determined to listen to Edward on strong beer (5-7)

indicators.note: In an across clue, X on Y puts X after Y, so HEAR TED follows STOUT.

blocks.note: Stout is a dark, strong beer.
To listen to is to hear.
Ted is a short form of Edward.

annotation.surface: Someone is set on hearing out Edward's views about strong beer.
annotation.walkthrough: The order differs from the surface: in an across clue, "on" places the listening and Edward after the beer, not before it.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone stout-hearted is brave and resolute, which is determined.

entries.clue: Vehicle taking another one up hill (7)

indicators.note: In a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so CART turns into TRAC.

blocks.note: A tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor.

annotation.surface: One vehicle tows another up a steep hill.
annotation.walkthrough: "Another one" means another vehicle, pointing back to the definition. A tor is a rocky hilltop in the West of England.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this heavy farm machine is one kind of vehicle, and it hauls loads just as the towing picture in the surface suggests.

entries.clue: Before ten, mail unfortunately not dispatched? Tough (13)

indicators.note: UNSENT comes before the mixed letters.
Something that went unfortunately went wrong, so the letters are rearranged.

annotation.surface: A worker grumbles that the post wasn't sent before ten, and that's tough.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is written in the order of the answer only once you notice "Before" applies to the second phrase: UNSENT goes before the rearranged TEN MAIL.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone unsentimental is hard-headed and tough.

entries.clue: Strike by footballer? / It tops the page (6)

blocks.note: A footballer strikes the ball with the head.
The running line printed along the top of every page of a document.

annotation.surface: A footballer's goal makes the top of the newspaper page.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are a football shot with the head and the running line at the top of a page.
annotation.definitionFit: A header is both a headed shot in football and the text at the top of a page.

entries.clue: Liable to slip up [with] account I had open, rent going astray (8-5)

indicators.note: Letters going astray wander out of place, so OPEN RENT is rearranged.

blocks.note: ACC is a short form of account.

annotation.surface: An account holder left the account open and the rent payment went missing.
annotation.walkthrough: I had shortens to I'd, giving ID without the apostrophe.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrase: a person who keeps having mishaps, tripping and dropping things, is described by this hyphenated adjective.

entries.clue: Test of divisions in society – not British (5)

indicators.note: Not British means leave out B.

blocks.note: Tribal describes divisions of society into tribes.
B is the standard abbreviation for British; it is removed.

annotation.surface: A sociologist tests how society is divided, excluding the British.
annotation.walkthrough: TRIBAL loses its B to leave TRIAL.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trial is a test of how something performs, as in a clinical trial or a trial run.

entries.clue: Waste a long time [in] underground prison (7)

annotation.surface: A prisoner wastes years locked below ground.
annotation.walkthrough: "Waste" looks like a verb in the surface; it is the noun dung.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the dark cell beneath a castle keep where captives were held.

entries.clue: Thin gooey stuff, almost (4)

indicators.note: Almost means not quite complete, so the last letter goes.

blocks.note: Slime is gooey stuff; its last letter is dropped.

annotation.surface: Something runny and gooey is nearly too thin.
annotation.walkthrough: "Thin" and "gooey" seem to describe the same liquid; thin is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe a slender figure, and both can also mean small, as in a slim or thin chance.

entries.clue: Lots [of] young men around ring (5)

indicators.note: Around means encircling, so the young men encircle the ring.

annotation.surface: Lots of young men gather round a boxing ring.
annotation.walkthrough: O stands for a ring because of its shape.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: both are casual ways of saying a great many, as in loads of time.

entries.clue: A disturbance when not starting sale (7)

indicators.note: Not starting means the first letter is dropped, so RUCTION loses R.

blocks.note: A ruction is a disturbance or row; its first letter goes.

annotation.surface: A commotion breaks out as a sale fails to get going.
annotation.walkthrough: A ruction is a noisy quarrel, a word more common in Britain than elsewhere.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this is one particular kind of sale, where buyers bid against each other and the highest offer wins.

entries.clue: Friend comes around in time finally [for] early show (7)

indicators.note: To come around something is to encircle it, so the friend wraps round the other letters.
Finally points to the last letter of time.

annotation.surface: A friend turns up just in time for the afternoon performance.
annotation.walkthrough: "In time" looks like one phrase meaning punctually; the setter uses its two words separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A matinee is an afternoon performance, earlier than the evening show.

entries.clue: Some wood elves do a lot of digging (5)

indicators.note: Some of the letters of wood elves give the answer.

blocks.note: The last letter of wood plus the first four of elves.

annotation.surface: Some woodland elves spend their time digging.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between wood and elves.
annotation.definitionFit: To delve is to dig, or to search deeply.

entries.clue: Street rodent seen round one narrow passage (6)

indicators.note: Seen round means placed on both sides of, so the rodent surrounds the one.

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street.
I is one as a Roman numeral.

annotation.surface: A rat is spotted in a street near a narrow alley.
annotation.walkthrough: The narrow passage is a sea channel, not an alleyway.
annotation.definitionFit: A strait is a narrow passage of water between two seas.

entries.clue: Singer [of] rap soon out of order (7)

indicators.note: Out of order means not in the right sequence, so the letters are rearranged.

annotation.surface: A singer's rap will soon be judged out of order.
annotation.walkthrough: "Out of order" reads as unacceptable in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this is one kind of singer, the highest female or boy's voice in a choir.

entries.clue: Bury an indefinite number put in prison (6)

blocks.note: In maths, n stands for an unspecified number.

annotation.surface: A number of people are buried or locked away.
annotation.walkthrough: n is used in maths for an unspecified number.
annotation.definitionFit: To intern is to confine someone, especially in wartime.

entries.clue: Variable beer served up with a lot of abuse (7)

indicators.note: In a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so ALE becomes ELA.
A lot of, not all of, STICK: the last letter goes.

blocks.note: Stick is abuse or criticism, as in taking stick; its last letter goes.

annotation.surface: A barman serves beer while enduring a torrent of abuse.
annotation.walkthrough: To give someone stick is British slang for criticising them.
annotation.definitionFit: Elastic means able to stretch or change, so variable.

entries.clue: Tries to have little time [in] suit (6)

indicators.note: To have something is to hold it, so the word for tries holds the little time inside.

blocks.note: A judge hears, that is tries, a case.
T is the abbreviation for time.

annotation.surface: Someone tries to find a little time for a legal suit.
annotation.walkthrough: "Tries" and "suit" point to the courtroom, but the suit is one of the four in a pack of cards.
annotation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four suits in cards.

entries.clue: Fool cutting exercise out? (5)

indicators.note: Cutting means slicing into, so the fool slices into the middle of the exercise.

annotation.surface: A fool skips the exercise class.
annotation.walkthrough: "Out" means out of fashion; "cutting exercise out" reads as dropping it.
annotation.definitionFit: Passé means out of date, out of fashion.

entries.clue: What will help one see small particles on the air (5)

indicators.note: Broadcast words are heard, not read, so the answer only sounds like the wordplay.

annotation.surface: Something to help one see dust floating in the air.
annotation.walkthrough: "On the air" seems to describe where the dust floats.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the answer is informal for spectacles, and glasses are exactly what will help one see.

entries.clue: Account for cross appearing in strange alpine (7)

indicators.note: X appears inside the other letters.
Strange suggests something odd, so ALPINE is rearranged.

annotation.surface: Someone must justify a cross planted somewhere unusual in the Alps.
annotation.walkthrough: X goes after the first letter of the rearranged ALPINE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to account for an event is to give the reasons behind it, as in accounting for a delay.

entries.clue: Number taken from sixty (4)

blocks.note: The surface reading is a subtraction sum; the meant reading is a numeral lifted out of a word.
Take letters from the word itself: its middle two form a Roman numeral.

annotation.surface: A number subtracted from sixty.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters IX sit inside sIXty, and IX is the Roman numeral for nine, which the grid wants written out in full.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the number: Roman IX is literally taken from the middle of the word sixty.

entries.clue: A more acceptable helper (7)

annotation.surface: One assistant is preferable to another.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A BETTER.
annotation.definitionFit: An abetter is someone who helps, usually in wrongdoing.

entries.clue: Frequently melt missing shillings (5)

indicators.note: Missing means without, so S is taken out.

blocks.note: To soften is to melt, as butter does.
S is the abbreviation for shillings, an old British coin; it is removed.

annotation.surface: Snow often melts, costing shillings.
annotation.walkthrough: A shilling was a pre-decimal British coin, abbreviated s.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean many times over, as in he often or frequently visits.

entries.clue: Close obscene broadcasting, [offering] redundancy (12)

indicators.note: Broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters are scattered.

annotation.surface: A regulator closes an obscene channel, leaving its staff redundant.
annotation.walkthrough: "Broadcasting" belongs with the TV picture, but here it scatters the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Obsolescence is the state of being no longer needed, redundancy.
